analysis.one_liner: Repeals every title of the 2010 Dodd-Frank financial reform law.
analysis.headline: A bill to repeal all of the Dodd-Frank financial reform law was introduced in April 2011 with 26 Republican sponsors, referred to the Senate Banking Committee, and never received a vote before that Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would have wiped out all fifteen titles of the Dodd-Frank Act, the 2010 law passed after the financial crisis. That law created the Consumer Financial Protection Bureau, required complicated derivatives to be traded on open markets, gave regulators power to wind down failing big banks instead of bailing them out, and set rules for credit rating agencies, mortgage lending, and credit card fees. The bill would have restored the rules as they existed before 2010. It never got a hearing or a vote.
analysis.who_benefits: If passed, large banks, hedge funds, and derivatives dealers would gain the most: they would be freed from Dodd-Frank's capital requirements, derivatives trading rules, and the Consumer Financial Protection Bureau's oversight of consumer lending. Credit rating agencies, payday lenders, and debt collectors would also lose their new oversight. Taxpayers would remain on the hook if a large institution failed, since the wind-down authority created to resolve failing banks without bailouts would disappear.

how_it_helps.text: Repeals titles I through XV of Dodd-Frank — the entire law — and restores the statutes as they existed before the 2010 reform [S2][S3].
Would eliminate the Consumer Financial Protection Bureau, restoring the pre-2010 patchwork of weaker consumer finance enforcement [S2][S3].
Would remove rules on derivatives, credit rating agencies, and the orderly liquidation authority used to wind down failing financial firms [S2][S3].

analysis.who_pays: If passed, ordinary consumers would pay: bank account holders, mortgage borrowers, and credit card users would lose the Consumer Financial Protection Bureau and the specific mortgage, fee, and lending rules Dodd-Frank created. Taxpayers would again be exposed to losses from a failing major financial institution, since the law's resolution authority would be gone. The memory of the 2008 crisis, which the 2010 law was written to prevent, was the reason supporters of the reform called this dangerous.

drawbacks.text: Dodd-Frank imposed significant compliance costs, and many community banks and smaller lenders said the paperwork burden fell on them even though they did not cause the crisis; full repeal would have lifted those burdens [S2][S3].

Some supporters of repeal argued that parts of Dodd-Frank, such as the designation of systemically important firms, encouraged concentration by advantaging the largest banks; full repeal would have removed that framework along with the rest of the law [S2][S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The cost side is enormous: the bill would have repealed the entire post-2008 regulatory response in one stroke, removing consumer protections, derivatives oversight, and the tools meant to let a failing giant bank be shut down without a taxpayer bailout. The benefit — relief for community banks from compliance paperwork — is real but narrow, and full repeal goes far beyond relieving small institutions. Repealing everything was a position few outside the sponsor bloc defended in detail.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was referred to the Senate Banking Committee on the day it was introduced, the committee never took it up, and it died there when that Congress ended in January 2013.

narrative.text: Senator Richard Shelby introduced the bill on April 6, 2011, joined by 25 other Republican senators including the party leader Mitch McConnell [S1][S3][S4].
It was read twice and referred to the Committee on Banking, Housing, and Urban Affairs on the day of introduction; no hearing, markup, or floor action ever followed [S5].
The 112th Congress ended on January 3, 2013, and the bill never received a vote [S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Because the repeal never happened, ordinary consumers and bank account holders kept the Dodd-Frank protections passed in 2010, and large banks did not get the deregulation they sought. The bill's sponsors were worse off than if it had passed.

for.name: Sen. Richard Shelby
for.role: U.S. Senator from Alabama and senior Banking Committee Republican
for.what_they_did: Introduced the full repeal of Dodd-Frank.

against.name: Senate Banking Committee (Democratic majority)
against.role: The committee the bill was referred to and never reported from
against.what_they_did: Took no action on the bill after its referral — no hearing, no markup, no vote.

sides.party_line_note: All 26 sponsors were Republican senators; no Democrat cosponsored the repeal [S4].

industries.industry: Large banks and financial holding companies
industries.note: Full repeal would free the largest banks from Dodd-Frank's capital rules, resolution authority, and systemically important firm oversight — rules written so their failure would not again require taxpayer bailouts. Their gain comes at the direct expense of the public's financial protections.
Dodd-Frank title VII required over-the-counter derivatives to be cleared and traded transparently; repeal would return that market to the opaque private dealing that amplified the 2008 crisis.

industries.industry: Payday lenders, debt collectors, and consumer finance companies
industries.note: Repealing the Consumer Financial Protection Bureau (title X) removes the single agency that polices these firms' treatment of borrowers; their gain is consumers' loss of that enforcement.
Dodd-Frank title IX imposed oversight on the agencies whose flawed ratings of mortgage securities fed the crisis; repeal would remove that oversight.

Full repeal would lift Dodd-Frank compliance burdens that smaller lenders said fell hardest on them, but it would also remove consumer protections in mortgage and card markets their customers rely on.
